newsitem.title: USA: Stock exchanges divided on move to decimal trading.
newsitem.headline: Stock exchanges divided on move to decimal trading.

text.p: U.S. stock exchanges are divided over a proposal to trade equities in dollars and cents instead of fractions.

Proponents argue that shifting to decimals would save investors billions of dollars by squeezing bid/offer spreads, the slight difference between the price at which a dealer will buy a stock and the price the dealer will sell the stock.

Most stocks are traded in eighths or sixteenths of a dollar, so the smallest bid/offer spread is 12.5, or 6.25 cents. Switching to decimals could, in theory, allow spreads to shrink to as little as one cent.

But the New York Stock Exchange warned in testimony before Congress Wednesday that converting prices from fractions to decimals would be costly and might undermine the critical relationship between public and professional traders.

"We believe there is no real evidence that decimal trading will benefit investors," exchange president William Johnston said in prepared testimony for the House Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials.
Smaller spreads could could facilitate frontrunning, a situation where a professional trader enters his own orders ahead of a trade for a public investor, Johnston added.

Under current exchange rules, "investors know that a professional trader must improve the bid or offer by a significant amount to establish priority over that customer," Johnston explained. "However, the smaller the tick becomes, the easier it would be for traders to step in front of other orders on an exchange."
Other exchanges took a different view, however. The Nasdaq and the Pacific Stock Exchange said they generally backed the move, but urged Congress to move slowly in imposing mandatory decimal trading.
"The Pacific Exchange supports decimal pricing," chairman Robert Greber said in prepared remarks.
After raising several concerns, Greber concluded "any proposal that enhances competitions and offers investors better prices ought to be carefully and deliberately pursued."
Nasdaq chief economist Dean Furbush said the all- electronic exchange is conducting a study to be completed in six months on the effects of decimal trading.
"Despite our favorable disposition, the NASD believes that the decision to decimalize should be made with great care and with full awareness of other priorities that will be displaced," Furbush said.

The American Stock Exchange, which has moved from eighths to sixteenths for some stocks, sees the move to decimals as "invevitable", president Thomas Ryan said in prepared testimony. But the exchange does not favor legislation "at this time", he added.
Major investors testifying at the hearing strongly backed the move to decimals.

"In my view, it is an anachronism that we must obtain and evaluate price quotes for shares in increments of eighths," said Herbert Dyer, executive director of the $40 billion State Teachers Retirement System of Ohio. "It suggests we are still wearing pantaloons, standing under oil lamps and biting coins to determine if the money is really gold."
